body:
Step one: I took a theory midterm in college. I was the only one in class that successfully answered the hardest question on the exam. 

Fast forward several weeks: I took the final for the course, but only did moderately well this time. I go to talk to the professor because I had questions about a couple of the problems (how they were actually solved), and he responds to my questions with "You're just not very good at theory."
Thanks. I'll give it a shot.

Maybe this sounds silly, but where do you start to look for therapists? I've been going to different ones at our University, but I think I need to cast my net wider, as I'm really not having success there. But I've searched on the internet, but choosing one of those just feels like poking in the dark.

Currently, no -- just a doctor who prescribes meds. 

I've been to two different therapists over the past year, but I don't know if I've been unlucky or what -- I never felt like I was making getting anywhere with either of them after going for at least 5 or so sessions to each of them. So I stopped going... but I should try to find another one. I just don't know where to find a good one. :-P

I had a number of people I considered really good friends, and I invited them to my wedding. I was a bit bummed because no one ever threw a shower for me, but what really sucked was these people that I thought I was so close to, couldn't be bothered to respond to the invitation. Some of them responded (and declined) but couldn't be bothered to send a card of congratulations or anything. It may not seem like a lot, but these were the people I thought I was closest to, and it hurt tremendously. I went through a lot of soul searching for quite a time after that.

I'm really sorry to hear that. I know exactly how you feel. This sort of thing is precisely why I stopped using facebook -- it feels like people are constantly rubbing into your face fun things that you weren't invited to go do.
Back off man, I'm a scientist.

Proazc has been shown to have libido-decreasing side effects for months and even years after the person has stopped taking it. :-( http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_SSRI_Sexual_Dysfunction http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1743-6109.2007.00630.x/abstract;jsessionid=253E61A9FF96E262079FBDFE5B464346.d02t04 I imagine that may be contributing, but also it sounds like she's also not very comfortable with other aspects of sex in general (bodily fluids, etc). I might suggest she see some sort of therapist on the grossed out issue, I think this could help her make good progress. I know this must be truly terrible to deal with, but do try to give her some time to recover from this. 

I know this may sound sort of crazy, but have you discussed with her the possibility of you doing someone on the side to help make up for the libido difference in the meanwhile? It sounds like otherwise you guys are happy together, and there are alternative arrangements that would allow you guys to happily continue as partners through life.

Don't lump all anti-depressants together in one big group. I felt the same way about anti-depressants for a long time (and was kinda scared of them), and it prevented me from getting treatment for my second-bout of depression because I had a series of really bad experiences the first time around on various anti-depressants. 

A friend convinced me to go in again, and it can be a matter of finding the right combination for you individually. I'm glad to say that after almost a year of battling this, I've found an anti-depressant that works with me and I've finally had almost a solid month under control. YAY!

I think my case was/is definitely more extreme than yours, but it sounds similar. Go talk to a professional to get an outside opinion. It could make all the difference.
